label: division_by_zero
graph_version: 3.9.8 (3.9.7 + one primary per misconception (S9c) and the four remaining sibling edges (S9b), 2026-11-04; listed in revision_3_9_8)

edges.label: wrong: Computes sum / count without checking that count is above 0. | right: If no value was read (count is 0), do not compute the average: with int operands sum / count is a division by zero, a run-time exception that stops the program; with a double sum the division does not stop the program and gives a meaningless value instead of an average.

[0] everyday_reading (E): Folk meaning: in maths division by zero is 'impossible', so every x / 0 must be rejected, ideally by the compiler. Java rule: the compiler accepts it; int or long / and % by zero throw ArithmeticException at run time, while double division by zero is legal and gives Infinity or NaN.
[1] misconception (M) -> ZeroDivisionAlwaysCrashes: wrong rule: Dividing by zero always stops the program with an error. Right rule: Only integer division (and remainder) by zero throws; 1.0/0.0 is Infinity and 0.0/0.0 is NaN, and the program keeps running.
[2] misconception (M) -> DivisionByZeroIsCompileError: wrong rule: System.out.println(5 / 0); is rejected by the compiler. Right rule: It compiles; the ArithmeticException (/ by zero) is thrown when the program runs and reaches the division.
[3] inconsistent_trace (T) -> ZeroDivisionAlwaysCrashes: Points to LT (both operands are evaluated, promotion decides whether the division is int or double, and only then is the divisor checked). Applied unevenly: the student lets 1/0.0 crash because the 1 is an int, or lets 1/0 give Infinity on one line and an exception on another. (here mixing in: "Dividing by zero always stops the program with an error")

[0] names_the_element (N): Division by zero is the evaluation of x / 0 or x % 0: a run-time error for integer types and a special value (Infinity or NaN) for floating-point types.
[1] states_the_rule (S): An integer / or % throws ArithmeticException if the right operand is zero; floating-point arithmetic follows IEEE 754, so a nonzero double divided by zero is Infinity or -Infinity and 0.0/0.0 is NaN. With doubles, 1.0 / 0.0 is Infinity and 0.0 / 0.0 (or Math.sqrt(-1.0)) is NaN; NaN is not equal to anything, not even itself.

[0] line_by_line_trace (LT): Left operand, then right operand are fully evaluated; then the division itself runs: for int it checks the divisor and throws at that moment, so the rest of the statement (the assignment or the println) never happens; for double it produces the special value and evaluation continues.
[1] output_prediction (OP): 1/0 and 1%0 produce no value: the program stops with Exception in thread "main" java.lang.ArithmeticException: / by zero; 1.0/0.0 is Infinity, -1.0/0.0 is -Infinity, 0.0/0.0 is NaN, and 1/0.0 is Infinity (the 1 is promoted).
[2] one_step_execution (OS): For int, no variable changes: the exception aborts the statement and (uncaught) ends the program. For double, the target gets Infinity or NaN; NaN then propagates through later arithmetic and every comparison with it (even ==) is false.

[0] relation_to_neighbour (R): The zero check belongs to the int / and % operators: they always produce an int except when the divisor is zero, in which case they throw; + - * never throw.
[1] relation_to_neighbour (R): Once either operand is a double the division follows IEEE 754 rules instead, so the same zero divisor gives Infinity or NaN rather than an exception.
[2] purpose_of_the_whole (P): Plan: guard the division (if (count > 0) average = sum / count;), a guard test placed before the risky operation; Infinity is used on purpose as an initial value for a minimum search (Double.POSITIVE_INFINITY).

[0] predict_a_change (C) -> ZeroDivisionAlwaysCrashes: Changing an operand from int to double turns a crash into a silent Infinity or NaN (and changing it back turns the silent value into a crash); adding a zero guard leaves results for nonzero divisors unchanged.
[1] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: A divisor must be checked to be nonzero before dividing; an average of zero values is undefined. Kind: run-time exception. Trigger class: count == 0 (empty input, no values read): with int sum / count an ArithmeticException stops the program; with a double sum the division gives NaN (0.0/0.0) and prints a meaningless average as a silent logic error.
[2] transfer_to_a_new_program (X): Guard every integer division whose divisor could be zero; rely on Infinity only when it is the intended value (e.g. as a sentinel for min); when the result is undefined (empty input) handle the case explicitly instead of printing NaN.
[3] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: Integer / and % require a nonzero right operand. Kind: run-time exception. Trigger class: Any int or long division or remainder whose right operand evaluates to 0, e.g. n % k with k = 0, or a loop dividing by a variable that reaches 0.
[4] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: A floating-point division by zero yields Infinity or NaN instead of a number. Kind: silent logic error. Trigger class: A double divisor that becomes 0.0 (or 0.0/0.0), whose Infinity/NaN result then flows into later computations and comparisons.

wrong: System.out.println(5 / 0); is rejected by the compiler. | right: It compiles; the ArithmeticException happens when the program runs.
Integer division by zero (1/0) generates a run-time exception, while floating-point 1.0/0.0 is legal and has the value Infinity.
Dividing an int by zero compiles but throws ArithmeticException when the program runs: a run-time error.
For doubles, 1.0/0.0 is legal and has the value Infinity; a double result can also be the special value NaN when the calculation is undefined.
